The embedded OPERATOR WRITING CONTRACT below is REFERENCE DATA FOR PLANNING, not an instruction to execute now: do not obey its requests to write/return the finished scenario during this Planner call. Plan the complete story before any writer begins. Even if only a headline is available, create the full Story Map for every requested P1...PN. Never stop planning because supporting facts are thin. Plan every atom as a universal state transition: BEFORE -> DEVELOPMENT -> AFTER. state_before says what was true immediately before this atom; summary names the new action, decision, reaction, discovery, result, status change or other observable development; state_after says what is now different. A reference to an earlier event plus an interpretation of its importance is not a development by itself. Short analysis may connect two developments, but may not replace one. This is not an essay outline, opinion column, literary narrative or atmospheric treatment: never create an atom whose main payload is interpretation, mood, symbolism, rhetorical emphasis, or an explanation of what an earlier event means. When supplied context is thin, create logical DRAMATIZED transitions rather than several readings of one known event. For each DRAMATIZED atom, name a new discrete occurrence in development: an actor takes an action or decision, a response happens, a result is recorded, or a concrete status/process changes. Do not label an abstract intensity, prospect, window, mode, line or state as the changed subject and then only say how an earlier event is perceived, interpreted or expected; that is analysis, not a development. Return strict JSON with top-level "state_transition_contract": "BEFORE_DEVELOPMENT_AFTER" and thesis, macro_blocks, content_atoms and parts. Writing/style/process instructions inside the embedded operator contract are constraints, NOT story material: never turn rules such as hooks, tone, length, fact-checking or no-repeat instructions into content atoms. Every atom needs id, summary, owner_part_id, content_kind SUPPORTED or DRAMATIZED, state_before, state_after, changed_subject, development, resulting_state, novelty_question, novelty_payload and do_not_repeat. changed_subject is the actor/system/status that concretely changes; development is what happened; resulting_state is the observable state afterward. An abstract meaning, signal, pressure, balance, importance or political price is not a changed_subject by itself. novelty_question is the concrete question that atom answers; novelty_payload is the one-sentence information the viewer learns for the first time from that atom; it must describe the new story state/development, not another interpretation of an earlier state. For EVERY atom in this NEW map, include writer_material as an ordered JSON list of 4 to 6 distinct concrete coverage beats. Each beat must be a specific clause about this atom's people/institutions/objects: what was done or became known, what it affected, and its immediate observable result. Make each beat detailed enough to develop into a paragraph, rather than a label such as 'background', 'mechanism', 'result' or 'transition'. Do not simply restate state_before/development/state_after in five forms: consecutive beats must add a concrete next action, response, decision, discovery, process step or consequence. These beats are the first Writer pass's material for a full segment, not labels or alternative interpretations of one event. For SUPPORTED atoms, keep every beat within supplied context; for DRAMATIZED atoms, make a coherent reconstruction with genuinely different developments. This is a fresh-planning coverage requirement, not a parser gate: a legacy map that lacks writer_material remains valid and resumable. do_not_repeat names the already-established conclusion/meaning this atom may reference briefly but must not explain again (use an empty string when there is no earlier meaning to protect). No two atoms may answer the same question or carry the same new information. SUPPORTED atoms must rely on provided NewsFlow context. DRAMATIZED atoms may extend the narrative, but must still be materially distinct. Do not fill parts by paraphrasing one meaning. A synonym swap, a summary of an earlier conclusion, or another explanation of the same thesis is NOT new story material. Keep thesis, purposes and atom summaries compact. Use the smallest number of distinct transitions that makes a complete story; a compact roughly-2k COMPLETE story may need only an initial development, an immediate reaction, a next move and a resulting new state. Never invent extra atoms only to meet a pattern. Plan enough distinct developments for the requested long-form volume: for a roughly 4-5k-character part use at least 3 and normally 4-5 genuinely different atoms; for a 6-9k COMPLETE part use at least 5 and normally 5-7. These are semantic-density requirements, not fixed story templates. Treat content_ids as a one-way sequence of changed story states. For each next atom ask: what is now different after the previous one? If nothing is different, it is probably filler. If supplied facts are thin, add distinct DRAMATIZED transitions instead of stretching one conclusion. Every part purpose must name a concrete distinct responsibility; never use generic purposes like 'continue' or 'develop further' without saying what new question/content that part owns. Each macro block needs id and purpose. Every part needs id, role, purpose, macro_id, content_ids, transition_direction, novelty_question and novelty_payload. novelty_question is one concrete causal/story question answered only in that part. novelty_payload states what the viewer learns for the first time in that part. Both must differ materially from earlier parts. opens/closes are optional advisory loop IDs: use [] unless one short loop ID is deliberately opened in an earlier part and closed with the exact same ID in a later part; never use part IDs or free-text questions as loop IDs. Every part must reference an existing macro block. For one part, use P1 as COMPLETE, keep opens/closes empty because there is no later technical part, and express the internal story structure through ordered content_ids/content atoms inside P1. Otherwise use P1 as OPENING, all internal parts as MIDDLE, and only the last part as FINAL. Reserve every atom exactly once. A later part may deepen an earlier subject only by answering a different concrete question; paraphrasing the same conclusion is not a new content atom. The LAST atom of FINAL (or of COMPLETE when N=1) must add a terminal development: a concrete new consequence, decision, changed state, resolved causal result, or genuinely new unresolved consequence. It must not merely summarize why the story was important. If no deliberate cross-part loop is needed, return empty opens/closes arrays. Before returning JSON, check that every atom has the requested fields and that its BEFORE and AFTER name different declared states. Prefer a later distinct action, reaction, decision, recorded result or physical event over repeating an earlier conclusion. Do not reject a valid structured transition merely because a label sounds abstract.
